theory.intro: For $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, the probability of exactly $r$ successes is $P(X=r)={}^{n}C_{r}\,p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$. The factor ${}^{n}C_{r}$ counts the orders in which the $r$ successes can fall, and each such order has probability $p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$.
facts: $P(X=r)={}^{n}C_{r}\,p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$ gives the probability of exactly $r$ successes in $n$ independent trials.
The exponent of $p$ is the number of successes $r$, and the exponent of $1-p$ is the number of failures $n-r$.
The two exponents always add to $n$, which is a quick check on any line of working.
Every order of $r$ successes and $n-r$ failures has the same probability, so the orders may be counted and then multiplied.
The factor ${}^{n}C_{r}$ is the number of ways the $r$ successes can be arranged among the $n$ trials.
Round only on the final line, to the accuracy the question asks for.
steps: Identify the success event, the number of trials $n$ and the probability of success $p$, and state $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$
Evaluate the combination and the two powers, then round as required

$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(9,0.45)$.

A biased spinner lands on red with probability $0.3$, independently on each spin.
It is spun $8$ times.
Find the probability that it lands on red exactly $5$ times, correct to four decimal places.

Find $P(X=6)$, correct to four decimal places.

Find $P(X=3)$, correct to four decimal places.

Each component made by a machine is defective with probability $0.06$, independently of the others.
A sample of $20$ components is taken.
Find the probability that exactly $2$ are defective, correct to four decimal places.

In a large city, $40\%$ of households own a dog.
Twelve households are chosen at random.
Find the probability that exactly $5$ of them own a dog, correct to four decimal places.

$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(15,\dfrac{1}{3}\right)$.
Find $P(X=6)$, correct to four decimal places.

$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(10,0.6)$.
Find $P(X=4)$, correct to four decimal places.

An inspector checks $14$ items, each independently faulty with probability $0.09$.
Find the probability that none of the items is faulty, correct to four decimal places.

A tennis player wins each of her service points with probability $0.72$, independently.
She serves $6$ points in a game.
Find the probability that she wins exactly $4$ of them, correct to four decimal places.

$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(13,0.5)$.
Find $P(X=6)$, correct to four decimal places.

A biased coin shows a head with probability $\dfrac{2}{3}$, independently on each toss.
It is tossed $9$ times. Find the probability of exactly $8$ heads as an exact fraction in lowest terms.
mastery.solution_text:
Success: the coin shows a head.
$X\sim\mathrm{Bin}\left(9,\dfrac{2}{3}\right)$
$P(X=8)={}^{9}C_{8}\left(\dfrac{2}{3}\right)^{8}\left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{1}$
$=9\times\dfrac{256}{6561}\times\dfrac{1}{3}$
$=\dfrac{2304}{19683}$
$=\dfrac{256}{2187}$
